1:
The divine speech Job has so long begged for at last breaks over him, and the witnesses gather first around the storm it comes in and the identity of the voice within it. The reformed John Gill hears the whirlwind raised on purpose to give notice that the Lord was about to appear, to display his majesty and command reverence; the Targum's name for it, "the whirlwind of distress," he takes as a mirror of the disturbed condition Job was in. And the speaker, Gill insists, is no created being but Jehovah the Son of God, the eternal Word, who very probably appeared in a human form, for there was an object seen as well as an articulate voice heard. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry orders the whole scene under a set of heads — who spoke, when, how, to whom, and what — and lands on the same identification: the Lord, Jehovah, not a created angel but the eternal Word himself, by whom the worlds were made, the same who afterwards spoke from Sinai, beginning here with the creation of the world as there with the redemption of Israel. When he spoke was "then," when the three friends and Elihu had all had their say and none had gained the point, so that it was time for God, whose judgment is according to truth, to interpose. How he spoke was out of the whirlwind, as a whirlwind had prefaced the visions of Ezekiel and of Elijah in 1 Kings 19:11, and as God is said to have his way in the whirlwind in Nahum 1:3 — the stormy wind made the vehicle of a voice perfectly audible even in its own noise.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses fix the word and the purpose. Adam Clarke observes that the storm is not the suphah of the preceding chapter but searah, something turbulent and violently agitated, a tempest meant to fill Job's mind with solemnity and an awful sense of the majesty of God; the Chaldee's "whirlwind of grief" would make the scene rather allegorical, impressed upon Job's imagination. John Wesley hears in that tempestuous wind the harbinger of God's presence, sent to awaken Job and his friends to a more serious attention and to testify his displeasure against them all, that every one might be the more deeply humbled. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott lifts the verse to its place in the book: this chapter is the grand climax and catastrophe of the poem, for the questions so fiercely debated could be solved only by the intervention of Him whose government was the very matter in dispute; and the one argument now developed, drawn throughout from man's ignorance, comes — though Job is afterwards justified in ch. 42:8 — in a tone from first to last mingled with reproach.
2:
The first question out of the storm is also its sharpest — "who is this that darkeneth counsel by words without knowledge?" — and the witnesses divide their attention between whom it strikes and why God must strike at all. The latin-fathers Gregory the Great supplies the deepest reason for the reproof. After the loss of his goods, the death of his children, the wounds of his body, his wife's evil counsel, and the insults of his comforters, all boldly borne, blessed Job might well have been praised by his Judge had he now been called out of this world; but since he is to receive back double and to live on in restored health, Almighty God is obliged to reprove him with strict justice, lest his very victory lay him low with the sword of pride. For nothing, Gregory says, more fatally slays a soul than the consciousness of virtue, which puffs it up and robs it of the fulness of truth; Job was just before his scourges and more just after them, raised the higher in the praise of God as he was smitten with the heavier chastisement, like a ductile tube lengthened by being hammered.

The reformed John Gill and the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch first settle who is meant. It is not Elihu, as some have thought, but Job himself whom the Lord answers and rebukes — inquiring, Gill says, not as one ignorant of him but as wondering that such a man should talk as he had, and angry enough to reprove it. Keil reads the Hebrew closely: the demonstrative zeh makes the interrogative "who" more vivid and pointed, and the participle "darkening" favours the assumption that Job has just uttered such words and is now interrupted by Jehovah, without any intervening speaker having come forward; the word is intentionally "counsel" for "my counsel," and the speech issues, by a mode of writing found only here and in ch. 40:6, "out of the storm."

The wesleyan-arminian voices press the charge home. Adam Clarke paraphrases it, Who art thou that pretendest to speak on the deep things of God and the administration of his providence, which thou canst not comprehend, and leavest my counsels the darker for thy explanation? John Wesley fixes the "counsel" as God's counsel — the very matter of the whole dispute, God's providence in afflicting Job, which Job had laboured to obscure — and marks how this first word struck Job to the heart, so that in his repentance he echoes it at ch. 42:3 as the arrow that stuck fast in him. The other grammatical-historical witness, Charles Ellicott, answers the question from Job's own mouth in ch. 14:1: it is a man, a dying and enfeebled creature, persecuted and exhausted as Job himself, altogether unequal to the task he has undertaken; and though "darkeneth counsel" points first at God's own counsel, such debate carried on in the ignorance of blind mortals cannot but seem, to the divine omniscience, the very darkening of counsel by words without knowledge.
3:
The reproof turns at once into a summons to the field: "gird up now thy loins like a man." The reformed John Gill hears the language of a soldier — a man of valour girding on his harness for battle — and reads it as a challenge to Job to prepare for the controversy the Lord was now entering into with him, and to bring forth his strong reasons and most powerful arguments in his own defence. The allusion, Gill notes, is to the custom of the eastern countries, where men wore long flowing garments and girded them close about the loins whenever they engaged in work or in war; Job had blustered what he would say could he but come face to face with God, and now he is dared to make his words good.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke softens the terror even as he sharpens the challenge. The Lord, he says, will not confound Job with his terrors; Job may dismiss all fearful apprehensions from his mind and now act like a man — kegeber, like a hero — stand up and vindicate himself. "For I will demand of thee" Clarke takes as the promise of a series of questions far easier of solution than the deep things Job had affected to discuss already, after which Job shall have his own opportunity to answer. And he pauses over the method itself: the most impressive and convincing manner of arguing, allowed on all hands, is that by interrogation, which the Almighty here adopts; the best orations of the ancients were framed after this manner, and Cicero's celebrated speech against Catiline, reckoned his masterpiece, opens with just such a multitude of short questions pressed closely one upon another. John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, adds only the soldier's image that governs the phrase — to gird up the loins as warriors then did before the battle.

The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the God who has been challenged to a hearing now grants it on his own terms, arraigning the man who would arraign him; and that the accuser who demanded an answer must first himself be questioned and made to answer, if he can. It is a reversal Job had half invited when he said, in an earlier and bolder mood, "call thou, and I will answer"; the Lord takes him at his word, and the interrogation that fills the rest of the chapter is the taking-up of that rash offer. The girding is not for flight but for a contest Job cannot win, and the very form of it — command met by command, challenge answered by a greater challenge — begins the humbling that will end in Job's hand laid upon his mouth.
4:
With the challenge laid down, the interrogation opens where creation itself began — "where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?" The reformed John Gill dwells on the paradox in the word "foundations": the earth has foundations so firm that it cannot be moved, yet what are they, since it hangs in the air upon nothing but the power and will of God, and the Son of God who upholds all things by the word of his power? Where was Job then? In a state of nothingness, a mere nonentity, not present when this amazing work was done nor witness to how the Lord went about it; and yet he takes upon himself to dive into the secret ways of Providence.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the verse a lesson in the greatness of God and the meanness of man. "I laid the foundations of the earth" proves him the only living and true God, a God of power in whom we may trust at all times; "where wast thou then?" exposes the contemptibleness of a creature who, for all the figure he cut among the children of the east, was so far from having any hand in the creation, or even from being a witness of it, that he was not yet in being — the first man was not, much less were we. It is the honour of Christ, Henry adds, that he was present when this was done, as the eternal Wisdom of Proverbs 8:22 and the Word of John 1:1; but we are of yesterday and know nothing. Let us not, then, find fault with God's works nor prescribe to him: he did not consult us in making the world, and yet it is well made; why should he take his measures from us in governing it?

The wesleyan-arminian voices keep the humbling brief and pointed. Adam Clarke sums the whole: thou hast a limited and derived being, thou art only of yesterday, what canst thou know? Didst thou see me create the world? John Wesley draws the same inference: thou art but of yesterday, and dost thou presume to judge my eternal counsels? — adding that God settled the earth as firm upon its own centre as if it had been built on the surest foundations. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks the art of the question: the very comparison of the creation of the world to the building of an edifice is a concession to the feebleness of man, one that of itself heightens the effect of the inevitable answer, for the man who was not there can only stand silent before the Architect who was.
5:
The building imagery is carried into the tools of the trade — the measuring-rule and the line — as the Lord asks who fixed the dimensions of the earth. The reformed John Gill puts the answer beyond question: not a creature but the Lord laid the measures, out in his divine mind and forth by his divine power, who does all things by weight and measure, settling how long and thick and broad the earth should be and where its borders should run. Job might know that God did this, Gill says, but not what the measures are: the mathematicians who pretend to give the circumference and diameter of the earth do not agree among themselves but widely differ, which shows they are at no certainty; and Job and the men of his age knew still less. The clause "if thou knowest," he adds, may even be rendered "for thou knowest," a severe sarcasm upon a man who set up to know so much.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the questions as pointing to an unfathomable depth of design. Who adjusted the earth's polar and equatorial distances from the centre? Who formed its zones and great circles, and proportioned its whole magnitude and gravity to the orbit in which it was to move, and its distance from that centre about which it revolves? These are questions, he says, that only show the difficulty of the subject and the depth of counsel in the earth's very framing. John Wesley keeps to the plain image: who prescribed how long and broad and deep it should be, and stretched the line — the measuring-line by which all its dimensions were regulated?

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the verse within the two-stage picture that governs these lines: the state of tohu va-bohu was the first half and the state of tehom the second half of the primeval condition of the forming earth, and the question passes over that watery chaos to the ordered work that follows, when foundations were sunk and a corner-stone laid. The witnesses do not divide. Whether they draw out the piety of a God who works by weight and measure, the astronomy of zones and orbits, or the philology of the primeval deep, they agree that the man challenged to name the earth's measures can only confess that he was neither the architect nor so much as a spectator of the plan.
6:
Still under the figure of a great building, the Lord asks after its foundations and its corner-stone, and the witnesses press the wonder that so vast a structure rests on nothing they can name. The reformed John Gill weighs the older guesses at what the "foundations" might be — the pillars of the earth, as Ben Gersom took them, or the mountains, as Aben Ezra understood them — but sweeps them aside with a question of his own: be they what they may, on what can they be fastened or sunk, when the earth hangs upon nothing, and there is nothing visible to support it, nothing but the mighty hand of God? It is the paradox of ch. 26:7, that he hangeth the earth upon nothing, brought to bear on the image of a founded house.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the question toward the science of his own day. How does the earth continue to revolve in the immensity of space? What supports it? Has it foundations like a building, and is it fastened with a key-stone to hold the mighty fabric in union? The questions are left open, as the Lord left them, to expose how little the questioner can answer. John Wesley draws the theology out plainly: this strong and durable building has no foundations but the power of God, which has marvellously established it upon itself; and the corner-stone, by which the several walls are joined and fastened together, is that in which, next to the foundations, the whole stability of a building consists. The sense, Wesley concludes, is simply this — who was it that built this goodly fabric, and established it so firmly that it cannot be moved?

The witnesses do not divide, and their very agreement makes the point of the verse. Man builds nothing that does not need a ground beneath it and a stone to bind the walls; and here is a house whose ground is the bare will of its Maker and whose corner-stone is his upholding word. If Job cannot tell upon what the foundations of the earth are fastened, still less can he prescribe to the God who fastened them; and the awe the image is meant to raise is the awe of a creature standing on a floor he did not lay, held up by a hand he cannot see. The building will stand, Gill and Wesley agree, because what God does is done for ever; and the same word that steadied the earth steadies the works of his providence, which no more than the world itself can be moved.
7:
The founding of the earth was no silent labour, for the Lord recalls the music that attended it — "when the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy." The reformed John Gill offers the fullest range of readings. The "morning stars" may be all the stars taken literally, for though strictly there is but one morning star, all may bear the name, being early created in the morning of the world, stars of light that shine till the morning and the nearer the morning the brighter, and which in their way praise God and set forth the glory of his perfections. Or they may be figures — the angels, as most interpret them, comparable to stars for their glory, purity, constancy, and number; or good men, the ministers and angels of the churches who are stars in Christ's right hand; while the principal morning star, Gill adds, is Christ himself.

The wesleyan-arminian voices settle on the angels. Adam Clarke argues that the words must refer to intelligent beings existing before the visible heavens and earth were made, the "morning stars" and the "sons of God" being one and the same angelic host, first though perhaps not chief in the order of creation, whose making may be included in the "heavens" of Genesis 1:1; the Chaldee reads "all the troops of angels," who witnessed the progress of the work and celebrated its wisdom and power in the highest strains. John Wesley agrees that the angels are well called morning-stars for their lustre and glory, and sons of God because they had their whole being from him and were made partakers of his image; and their shouting, he notes, intimates that they neither advised nor assisted in the work, nor censured any of it, as Job had presumed to do.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott concurs that the context points to the angels entrusted with the stars' guardianship, from whom Milton borrowed his conceptions, and adds that the magnificent sublimity of the expression needs no comment. So the witnesses genuinely part over what the morning stars are — Gill allowing the literal stars, or the ministers, or Christ, alongside the angels, while Clarke, Wesley, and Ellicott take them simply as the angelic choir. Yet on the point of the verse they meet: whatever sang, it sang the Creator's praise and not its own, and the joy that greeted the laying of the earth's foundations is the very reverse of the fault-finding Job has fallen into, who would arraign the counsels the angels adored.
8:
From the founded earth the survey turns to the sea, and the Lord asks who shut it up with doors when it broke forth as from the womb. The reformed John Gill reads the whole picture as belonging to the sea's first creation, not to the later flood, and finds it drawn throughout as an infant: here the sea is still in embryo, shut up in the bowels of the earth where it was first laid, as a child is shut within its mother's womb, and closed in with doors. The bowels of the earth, Gill says, were the storehouses where God first laid up the deep waters, and the misshapen chaos was like a woman big with child, ready to be delivered of the ocean.

The wesleyan-arminian voices dwell on the birth-metaphor and its exactness. Adam Clarke calls it a very fine figure: the sea is a newly born infant issuing from the womb of the void and formless chaos, and even the delicate circumstance of the waters that burst forth before the birth is alluded to, an image the next verse will carry on. John Wesley asks the question the verse presses: who was it that set bounds to the vast and raging ocean and shut it up, as with doors, within its proper place, that it might not overflow the earth? — brought forth, as it were, from the womb or bowels of the earth into the channel God had appointed for it.

The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse with one mind as the taming of the sea at its very birth. There is a tenderness in the figure that offsets its grandeur: the ocean, terror of mariners and image of all that is unruly, is handled by its Maker as a nurse handles a new-born babe, delivered, shut in, and given its bounds. And the point for Job is plain enough. He who could not tell where he was when the earth was founded was as little present at the sea's nativity; the doors that hold back the flood were hung by a hand not his, and the same word that said to the waters "thus far" holds them still. The proud and heaving deep, so far from being beyond God's control, came forth at his bidding and was swaddled at his will, and the man who would question the government of the world was not so much as a witness to the shutting of its first great door.
9:
The birth-figure is carried into the sea's first clothing, "when I made the cloud the garment thereof, and thick darkness a swaddlingband for it." The reformed John Gill keeps the metaphor tight: the cloud is the garment for this new-born babe, the sea. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the lines in the same key, God putting clouds round the sea as a garment and thick mist as its swaddling-clothes, part of the ordered sequence by which the deep, having broken from the womb, is wrapped, bounded, and laid to rest.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses draw out the delicacy of the image. Adam Clarke sees an allusion to the very cloth in which a new-born infant is first received: the cloud was to the newly raised vapour what the receiving-cloth is to the child, and the thick darkness a swaddlingband, recalling the first dressings of an infant, who is swathed to support a body too tender to bear even careful handling without some medium between the nurse's hand and its flesh. The image, Clarke quotes Mr. Good as saying, is exquisitely maintained — the new-born ocean issuing from the womb of chaos, and its dress that of a new-born infant; and there is here an allusion also to the creation of Genesis 1:2, where darkness was upon the face of the deep, so that the thick darkness becomes a swaddlingband for the new-born sea. John Wesley reads it the same way: God covered the sea with the vapours and clouds that rise out of it and hover above it, covering it like a garment; the black and dark clouds are its swaddling-bands, keeping the great infant within its bounds — though in truth, Wesley adds, neither clouds nor air nor sands nor shores can bound the sea, but God alone.

The witnesses do not divide; the metaphor governs them all. What in nature looks like mere cloud and gloom over the water is, in the divine speech, the tender apparatus of a nursery: the God who delivered the sea also dressed it, wrapping the wildest of his creatures in cloud and dark as a mother wraps her child. And the lesson for the questioner is folded into the swaddling-bands. Job, who could not so much as name the garment of the sea, is in no position to loosen the counsels of the God who clothed it; and the very tenderness of the figure rebukes his complaint, for the hand that swaddles is not the hand of an enemy but of one who cares even for the deep.
10:
The swaddled sea is next given its cradle and its prison, as the Lord recalls how he "brake up for it my decreed place, and set bars and doors." The reformed John Gill, following Broughton's rendering "and brake the earth for it by my decree," sees God cleaving the earth to make a vast chasm to hold the waters — raising the hills and sinking the valleys, so that these became the channels to convey the waters to their appointed place; a cradle, as it were, prepared to receive the swaddled infant, in the work of the second day of creation.

The wesleyan-arminian voices attend to the bars and doors. Adam Clarke refers the "decreed place" to the word of Genesis 1:9, "Let the waters be gathered together unto one place, and let the dry land appear": the dry land itself forms the bars and doors of the sea, everywhere a barrier against its encroachments, while the great rivers, bays, and creeks are the doors by which it passes into the interior of continents. John Wesley reads the same: God made the hollow places in the earth to serve as a cradle to receive and hold this great infant when it came from the womb, and fixed its bounds as strongly as if they were fortified with bars and doors.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the wording, preferring "and prescribed for it my decree" — that is, determined the boundaries of its abode — and marvels at the fact behind the phrase: when we bear in mind the vast forces and the unstable nature of the sea, it seems a wonder that it acknowledges any limits at all, and is held in restraint by them. Gill and Wesley are careful to keep the tenderness of the figure alongside its power: the chasm is not only a prison but a cradle, sunk on purpose to receive the great infant when it came from the womb, so that the same act which shuts the sea in also lays it down to rest.

The witnesses do not divide. Cradle and prison are one thing here, for the same broken chasm that receives the sea also confines it, and the same shores that rock it also shut it in. Job, who was not there when the valleys were sunk or the bars set, cannot loosen the decree that keeps the ocean in its bed; and the God who prescribed a bound to so mighty and so restless a thing has surely prescribed a bound as well to the afflictions Job would have him lift, which rise no higher and roll no further than his word allows. What looks like the mere shape of coasts and sea-floors is, on the witnesses' reading, a decree and a discipline: the deep is held to its place, and so, they imply, is every troubling thing the Lord has made.
11:
The decree spoken to the sea is at last put into words — "hitherto shalt thou come, but no further: and here shall thy proud waves be stayed." The reformed John Gill hears in it the very voice of command: the waters shall spread to such and such shores and wash them, but go no further; their rolling tides shall run up so far into the rivers that issue from them and then return, keeping exactly to their time and place. This, Gill insists, is said by Jehovah the Word of God, and through his almighty power it is attended to; the proud waves obey a sentence they cannot pass.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns to the machinery by which so vast a restraint is worked. "Hitherto shalt thou come" fixes the reach of the sea's flux and reflux, and the tides, he shows, are marvellously limited and regulated — partly by the attraction of the sun and moon, partly by the earth's rotation, which carries some thousand and forty-two miles of the equator past any point of the heavens in an hour, and about five hundred and eighty in the latitude of London, so that the attracted waters are continually passing from under the direct pull that would raise them. The bars and doors, on his reading, are these very laws: the attraction of sun and moon on the one hand, and the gravitation of the sea's own parts to its centre on the other, prevent at once too great a flux and too deep an ebb; the spring-tides come at the change and full of the moon, the neap-tides between, and a whole world of wisdom and management was needed to proportion all these forces to each other. What Gill hears as a bare word of command, Clarke traces through the mechanics of the tides, yet both arrive at the same wonder.

The witnesses do not divide; the reformed piety and the wesleyan natural philosophy meet on the one confession. Whether the sea is stayed by the naked fiat of the eternal Word or by the balanced pull of moon and sun and the spinning of the globe, the staying is God's, and the proud waves that seem to threaten the shore twice a day are in truth kept back by a decree they cannot break. For Job the moral is the same as for the mariner: the God who has set an unpassable bound to the ocean's pride is the God whose government of the world, and of one suffering man within it, is neither careless nor overmastered, but holds every heaving thing to its appointed line.
12:
The Lord now leaves the sea for the sky, and asks whether Job in all his years ever "commanded the morning" or taught the dayspring its place. The reformed John Gill fastens on the impotence the question exposes: Job had lived to see many a morning, but it never lay in his power to command one; he had been in such straits as to long for the morning light before it came, yet was obliged to wait for it, unable to hasten it or make it spring before its time. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, opening here his account of the "six things" the Lord challenges Job to explain, dwells on the same helplessness: the morning-light is not commanded since our days, but what it is, it was long before we were born, neither made by us nor designed primarily for us; the dayspring knew its place before we knew ours, for we are but of yesterday. It is quite out of our power to alter that course — we cannot raise the morning sooner than its time to serve our turn, nor order the dayspring to any other place than its own — and the constant, regular succession of day and night is no contrivance of ours but the glory of God and his handiwork, as Psalms 19:1 declares. Whether the morning-light was meant to figure the gospel of Christ Henry will not say, but he cannot help hearing in it the dayspring from on high that has visited us in Luke 1:78.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses turn to the astronomy of the dawn. Adam Clarke refers "commanded the morning" to the twilight caused by the refraction of the solar rays through the atmosphere, by which we receive the light by degrees that would otherwise burst upon and injure the eye; and "caused the dayspring to know his place" he reads of the shifting points at which day breaks through the year, as the earth's annual revolution carries the sun north and south of the equinoctial, so that dawn rises at no two successive days in the same point of the horizon. John Wesley asks simply whether Job created the sun and appointed the order and succession of day and night — a work done long before he was born — and whether he taught the dayspring the punctual time and the point of the heavens at which it should arise, which varies every day.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the observation in a phrase: the dayspring is caused to know its place, changing as it does from day to day with the changing seasons. The witnesses do not divide. Piety, meteorology, and philology alike converge on the one truth — that the man who cannot advance the morning by a single minute, nor shift the point of its rising by a hair, is in no case to prescribe to the God who commands it.
13:
The morning is given a moral office as well as a natural one, taking hold of the ends of the earth "that the wicked might be shaken out of it." The reformed John Gill notes how swiftly the office is done: as the morning light springs forth it quickly reaches the extreme part of the hemisphere; and he cannot help applying it to the light of the gospel, directed under Providence to the very ends of the earth. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the image its physical force: the dawn, spreading out from a single point, takes hold of the carpet of the earth as it were by the edges and shakes off from it the evil-doers who had laid themselves down upon it the night before; the verb, they note, combines the senses of thrusting and of shaking. Charles Ellicott, the other grammatical-historical voice, fixes the same figure precisely: it is that of a man shaking out a cloth, as at ch. 24:15-17.

The wesleyan-arminian voices name who is shaken. Adam Clarke pictures the thieves, assassins, murderers, and adulterers who hate and shun the light flying, as the dawn breaks, like ferocious beasts to their dens and hiding-places; and he judges that the fifteenth verse belongs immediately with this one, its connection disturbed by the intervening fourteenth, so that "from the wicked their light is withholden" follows straight upon their being shaken out — for they love darkness, prowl by night, and are driven to sleep by day. John Wesley reads the verse the same way: the morning-light spreads in a moment from one end of the hemisphere to the other, and its effect upon the wicked is to shake them from the face of the earth, both because it discovers them, whereas darkness hides them, and because the morning is the usual time for executing judgment.

The witnesses do not divide over the picture, though Clarke stands somewhat apart in reordering the lines to bind verse thirteen to verse fifteen. What they share is the sense of the dawn as a minister of justice: the same light that is the comfort of the honest is the terror of the guilty, and the God who each morning shakes the earth like a garment to rid it of its vermin is the Judge whose light no evil-doer can endure. Job, who had himself observed in ch. 24:13 what a terror the morning is to criminals, is here shown that the world owes that mercy not to him but to the great Judge who sends the beams of the morning as his messengers to detect and to arraign.
14:
The same dawn that shakes out the wicked works a transformation on the face of the earth, which "is turned as clay to the seal, and they stand as a garment." The reformed John Gill draws out the first figure: as clay takes a new form under the impress of the seal, so the earth appears in a wholly different character when the morning light comes upon it. In the darkness of night nothing of its form or beauty is to be seen — it is a mere tohu and bohu, like the chaos, its rising hills and spreading dales and beautiful landscapes hidden; but when the light breaks forth it is seen in all its beauty and glory, and Gill hears in the change an emblem of the change the gospel light makes in men.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lingers over the seal and the garment. The earth, like soft clay, is capable of taking endless forms, as its astonishing variety of plants and flowers and fruits attests; and he sees an allusion to the sealing of clay still common in the East, having before him six Eastern brass seals, their figures cut in relief, once used for stamping pottery. Receiving the impressions of the solar light and heat, the earth's plants and flowers spring up and decorate its surface like a richly stamped garment upon a person. Clarke pauses to correct Mr. Good, who would render the clay as bent round a mould: rays of light, he objects, never bend but travel in a straight course, so that a gun might as well be expected to shoot round a corner as a ray to follow the windings of a tube; the metaphor holds only as the sun advances in his daily round and successively invests every part of the earth's surface with light.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders it "changed as clay under the seal, and all things stand forth as in their proper raiment": in darkness every object is without form and void, like clay or wax that has no shape till the seal is applied, and then the impression is clear and manifest. John Wesley reads it to the same effect — the seal makes a beautiful impression on clay that of itself has no form, and so the earth, which by night lies like a confused heap, when the light arises appears in excellent order and glory, its men and things and living creatures presenting themselves to view, clothed and adorned as with a garment. The witnesses do not divide over the picture, though Clarke alone turns aside to the optics of it; they agree that the morning re-creates the world's beauty daily, stamping a form on what the night had left formless, and that the God who so easily new-dresses the earth every dawn is no fit subject for the complaints of a man who cannot make a single flower stand up.
15:
The morning's office of justice is completed as, from the wicked, "their light is withholden, and the high arm shall be broken." The reformed John Gill fixes the paradox of the phrase: the light that is withheld from the wicked is the darkness that had been their light, for their day is the night, and the coming of the morning deprives them of it. Yet he hears a deeper sense beneath the literal one. The "light" withdrawn may be the light of their prosperity, taken from them; or it may be the light of life itself, when at last they are sent into utter darkness. Either way, the dawn that comforts the honest is the undoing of the wicked, robbing them of the covering they loved.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley weighs the two ways the light comes to be withheld. That light which others enjoy is withholden from the wicked, he says, either by their own choice, because they choose darkness rather than light and cannot bear the day that discovers them; or else by the judgment of God, or of the magistrate who acts in his name, by whom they are cut off from the light of the living altogether. And the "high arm" that shall be broken Wesley reads as their great strength — the arm they had lifted up and used for the oppression of others — now shattered, so that they are stripped at once of their concealment and of their power to do mischief.

The witnesses do not divide, and between them they trace the whole ruin of the evil-doer at the break of day. His inverted world is overturned: the darkness that served him for light is snatched away, whether by his own flight from the discovering beam or by the sentence of a Judge who has appointed the morning for the executing of justice; and the arm that was raised against God and man, so strong in the covering dark, is broken in the open light. There is a sober warning in it for every reader, but there is comfort too in the shape of the thing, for it shows the morning to be no blind or indifferent power but the servant of a moral order. The God who each day withholds the wicked's light and breaks the oppressor's arm is the God whose government Job would arraign; and the very regularity of the dawn, so gentle to the upright and so fatal to the guilty, is a daily witness that the world is ruled in righteousness by a hand Job cannot see but cannot escape.
16:
Leaving the sky, the Lord plunges Job into the deep, asking whether he has entered the springs of the sea or walked in the search of its depth. The reformed John Gill canvasses the many renderings the words have borne: the "springs" may be the subterranean passages through which the waters flow in to supply the sea, or the fountains that rise at its bottom, where some report even springs of sweet water; the phrase has been read as "the drops of the sea," or, following the Targum, as its "perplexities" — the thickets, woods, and forests some imagine there, or the shelving rocks and sandy mountains, or the utmost borders of the deep. Whatever the reading, Gill turns each into the same unanswerable challenge: has Job entered these, travelled the main ocean, and gone to its farthest bounds?

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke owns that of these springs, inlets, and outlets we know just as much as Job. Some philosophers, he notes, supposed the sea supplied through a porous bottom by fresh matter continually oozing up — though such pores might as well let the water out as in. And "walked in the search of the depth" he takes literally: has Job walked from the shallow beach through the whole bed of the ocean to its profoundest depths? No man since him has found them out, and in multitudes of places the sea is unfathomed by any line hitherto let down. John Wesley notes that the Hebrew of "springs" is literally "the tears" of the sea, the fountains out of which its waters flow as tears from the eyes; and he draws the argument home — if Job cannot find the utmost depth of the sea, which in many places the wisest mariner could never reach, how then can he fathom the depths of God's counsels?

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott would rather read the "springs" as the mazes and intricacies of the trackless, pathless deep, and "the search of the depth" as its secret recesses; and this, he observes, leads on to the cognate thought of the bottomless pit of death in the verse that follows. So the witnesses part a little over the very word — subterranean springs, or the sea's "tears," or its trackless mazes — but they meet in the one confession the verse is built to draw: that the deep keeps its secrets from the man who would sound the counsels of its Maker, and that the ocean he cannot search is a fit emblem of the providence he cannot fathom.
17:
From the sea's depth the questions descend further still, to death itself: "have the gates of death been opened unto thee? or hast thou seen the doors of the shadow of death?" The reformed John Gill is careful about which gates are meant — not those by which death entered the world, sin and the divine appointment and the calamities that occasion it, but those by which men pass into the state of the dead. Men know not experimentally what death is, Gill says, nor in what way, nor at what time, nor in what place they shall go out of the world; they know not the state of the dead, which holds no correspondence with the living; and the gates of that dark and invisible region have never been thrown open for mortals to look within.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the parallel members closely — were the gates of death unveiled to thee, and didst thou see the gates of the realm of shades? — carrying the survey down into the underworld as the next questions will carry it across the breadth of the earth. Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian voice, presses the mystery to a point: dost thou know in what the very article of death consists? It is as inexplicable a question as "what is animal life?" And he marks the two words the verse distinguishes, maveth, death, and tsalmaveth, the shadow of death, the intermediate state, the openings into the place of separate spirits; it will not do, he adds, to call death the mere privation of life, for what then would the shadow of that privation be?

John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, gathers the whole into a meditation on death as a grand secret. We know not when or by what means we shall be brought to it, by what road we must go the way whence we shall not return; we cannot describe how the knot is untied between soul and body, nor how the spirit goes to be we know not what and live we know not how; we hold no correspondence with separate souls, and speak of the world of spirits as blind men do of colours, only to be amazed, when we remove thither, at how much we were mistaken. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that death, so near to every man and so certain, is yet a sealed country to the living, and that the man who has never seen its gates opened is in no position to demand the reasons of the God who holds their keys.
18:
The survey comes back to the surface with a question that might seem the most answerable of all: "hast thou perceived the breadth of the earth?" The reformed John Gill takes "breadth" as standing for all the earth's dimensions — its length, breadth, diameter, and circumference, but especially the measure of its surface. Has Job gone over the whole face of it and measured its every part, its hills and dales, its rocks and mountains, and taken the survey of all its cities and towns and villages, its woods and forests, its fountains and rivers? If a man lived as long as Methuselah, Gill answers, and spent all his days at the task, he could never accomplish it; and some parts of the earth are simply inaccessible, not to be measured by the most skilful geometer.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets the question in its ancient horizon. At the time it was asked, the circumference of the globe was not known, the earth itself being supposed a vast extended plain, bordered all round with the ocean and the sky. What Job could not measure, he could not even rightly conceive. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott would render the verb "comprehended" rather than "perceived," and agrees that the earth is here thought of as a vast plain, as the shaking figure of the earlier verse also implied. Yet he adds a striking observation: unscientific as all this language is, its majestic sublimity is not one whit affected by it. The picture may belong to an older cosmology, but the awe it commands is untouched.

The witnesses do not divide, and their agreement carries the argument a step further than the others. It is one thing to be ignorant of the deep sea or the far heavens or the state of the dead; but here Job is challenged upon the very ground he walks, the earth given to the children of men, and even this he cannot compass or comprehend. The most level and homely of the divine questions defeats him as surely as the loftiest. And Ellicott's point sharpens the rebuke: the sublimity of God's works does not wait upon the accuracy of man's science, so that Job's inability to measure the earth is no mere gap in his knowledge but a standing proof that the creature who cannot span the plain beneath his feet has no business diving into the depth of his Maker's counsels.
19:
The interrogation rises again to the mystery of light, asking after the very dwelling of light and darkness: "where is the way where light dwelleth? and as for darkness, where is the place thereof?" The reformed John Gill reads it as an inquiry after the road to the place where light has its home, and what that place may be — a home no traveller has found. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the question into a probe of natural philosophy that his own age could no better answer than Job's. What is the source of light? Light was before the sun, so what is light itself — a substance, no doubt, but of what kind, and of what particles? And as for darkness, what is it? Is it even philosophical, Clarke asks, to call it the mere privation of light? Philosophy will have made some real advance, he judges, when it can tell us what cold is and what darkness is, leaving mere privations out of the question.

John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, unfolds the verse as a string of the very questions God means Job to feel unable to answer. Where does light keep its constant and settled abode? Whither goes the sun when it departs from this hemisphere — where is the tabernacle or the chamber in which it is supposed to rest? And since there was a time when there was nothing but gross darkness upon the face of the earth, what way came light into the world at the first, from what place was it fetched, and whence came that orderly constitution and constant succession of light and darkness? Was this Job's work? Was he so much as privy to it, a counsellor or an assistant when it was done?

The witnesses do not divide. Light and darkness are here personified as dwelling each in its own place, and the whole force of the verse lies in the fact that Job knows the road to neither. Clarke's frank confession that the learning of centuries has not told us what light is only underlines the ancient point: the man who cannot say what light is, nor where it lodges, nor by what way it first came into a dark world, is confounded by the plainest and most familiar of God's creatures. And if the dwelling of the light that visits him every morning is past his finding out, the counsels of the Father of lights, which were from eternity, are further past it still.
20:
The question of light's dwelling turns to a mocking commission: that Job "shouldest take it to the bound thereof, and know the paths to the house thereof." The reformed John Gill reads it as a challenge to take the light — or the darkness, but rather the light — as it were by the hand and guide it to its utmost bound; a thing only the Lord can do and does. For he has set a tabernacle for the sun, which goes forth at his command like a strong man to run a race, whose going forth is from the end of the heavens and his circuit to the ends of it, so steered and directed by God that it never misses its way nor errs from its path, but keeps exactly to its rising and its setting and its appointed bound.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears in it a strong and biting irony. To "take it to the bound thereof" is, with Mr. Good, to lay hold of the light in its very boundary — to go to the precise spot where light commences and darkness ends and see the house where each of them dwells. Darkness and light are here personified, Clarke says, each as a real and intelligent being with a separate existence and a local dwelling, for poetry animates everything, and this is the region of fictitious existence. He would render the verse itself with the irony laid bare: "For thou canst take Us to its boundary; for thou knowest the paths to its house" — a taunt whose whole design is to humble Job's knowing pride and send him to seek true wisdom and humility where they are to be found. Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, glosses the phrase more soberly: "that thou shouldest take it" means to go with, or to track, the light to its home.

John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, keeps to the plain sense — to bring or lead the light, and darkness as the consequent of it, over its whole course from the place of its supposed abode to the journey's end, and to know where a man might find it and whence he might fetch it. The witnesses do not divide over the meaning, though Clarke alone insists on hearing the sarcasm in it. Together they make the verse a study in the impossibility of the errand: the light Job cannot even define he is ironically bidden to escort to its lodging and back, and the very absurdity of the commission is the measure of how far he stands from the God who does, in fact, lead the light forth and home again every day of the world.
21:
The irony that has been rising through these verses now breaks openly, in a line that reads as a taunt: "knowest thou it, because thou wast then born? or because the number of thy days is great?" The reformed John Gill takes the words at their face and lets the impossibility answer itself. Was Job present when light and darkness were first separated and had their several apartments assigned them, their laws given and their bounds set? He was not; and had he been the very first man, he still could not have been early enough to witness it, since man was not made until the sixth day of the creation, when the work was already done. To know these things by having seen them, a man must have been born before the world.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears the verse as another strong and biting irony, and finds the sarcasm confirmed by the plainest translation: "Thou knowest, because thou wast then born, and the number of thy days is great" — multitudinous, he notes, rabbim, as though Job's years were beyond counting. The Lord speaks as if crediting Job with an age that reaches back before the light, precisely to expose how absurd such a credit is. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agrees, and would read the whole verse without the interrogation, as sublime irony: "Doubtless thou knowest all this, for thou wast born then, and the number of thy days is so great!"

Here the witnesses touch a small but real difference of reading. Gill keeps the interrogative form the Authorised Version gives, a question whose expected answer is a shamed silence; Clarke and Ellicott would drop the question-mark altogether and let the words stand as a flat, ironic statement, mock-praise of Job's supposed antiquity. Yet the difference is only in the pitch of the voice, for both readings serve the one end. The verse turns the humbling of v.4 — "where wast thou?" — into open mockery: a creature of yesterday, made on the last day of the creation week, is gravely asked whether he remembers the dividing of the light, and the very form of the asking, whether taken as question or as sarcasm, leaves him nothing to say. The man who would reason with God about counsels that were from eternity is reminded that he was not present even at the making of the morning.
22:
The Lord opens his storehouses next, asking whether Job has entered "the treasures of the snow" or seen "the treasures of the hail." The reformed John Gill explains why the word is treasures: the vapours raised and the clouds formed in the atmosphere are the storehouse of these meteors, and they are called treasures because they are hidden there and unseen by man until they fall, because they are at the command and keeping of the Lord, and because they are rich and enriching — snow especially, which falling keeps the earth warm and makes it fruitful, and both of which come in such abundance. Yet Gill is careful to guard the figure: we are not to imagine that God has literal heaps of snow and hail laid up in store from times past, but that he can produce them as easily and as suddenly, when he pleases, as one who has treasures laid up can bring them forth at once.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns to the formation of the two. It is easier, he grants, to account for snow than for hail: hail is generally supposed to be drops of rain frozen in their passage through cold regions of the air, yet it is found composed of many small spherules frozen together, its centre sometimes soft like snow and sometimes a hard nucleus. Both snow and hail, he holds, owe their formation to electricity, the hail formed in the higher regions where the cold is intense and the electric matter abundant. And he notes a curiosity of Providence: hail is the one meteor of this kind from which no apparent good is derived, for whereas rain and dew give life, and frost pulverizes and fertilizes the soil, and snow covers and defends the tender plants, hail does none of these but often much harm, chilling and blasting in spring and summer — frost being, as he finely puts it, God's universal plough. John Wesley keeps to the wonder of the storehouse, asking whether Job knows where God has laid up those vast quantities of snow and hail which he draws forth whenever he sees fit.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill's theology of the "treasures," Clarke's meteorology of the frozen spherules, and Wesley's plain awe all serve the single argument: the snow and hail that answer so exactly to their Maker's purposes are stored beyond Job's sight and drawn out beyond his power, and the man who has never entered these treasuries cannot pretend to order the God who keeps their keys.
23:
The stored snow and hail prove to be an armoury, "reserved against the time of trouble, against the day of battle and war." The reformed John Gill reads the reservation plainly, as kept for the punishment and affliction of men, held ready for the hour God appoints. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the whole passage forward in their rendering — the snow and hail reserved for a time of trouble, the way by which the light is parted, the watercourse cleft for the overflowing waters and the path for the lightning of thunder — and pause on the deeper principle of the following lines, that rain and dew have no created father and ice and hoar-frost no created mother, the parallel questions asking after the one who begets and the one who bears.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes both the wording and the history. "Reserved against the time of trouble" he renders as the season of strictness, when the earth is constringed and bound by the frost; and "the day of battle and war" he refers to the hailstones that have served as instruments of God's displeasure against his enemies, with a plain allusion to the plague of hail sent upon Egypt in Exodus 9:23, and to the destructive shower that fell upon the Canaanitish kings in Joshua 10:11. Charles Ellicott, the other grammatical-historical voice, points to the same battle, when the LORD cast down great stones from heaven upon the fleeing kings, and compares the hail and coals of Psalms 18:13.

The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the snow and hail are not merely stored but stationed, an arsenal kept in reserve for the day of God's controversy with a rebellious world. What looks to man like idle weather is, to the eye of the divine speech, ammunition laid up against an appointed war; the God who fought for Israel from the sky at Beth-horon can fight as effectually with snow and hail as with the sword of an angel. And the argument presses hard upon Job. He who cannot so much as enter these treasuries, still less command their contents, is confronted with a God armed with the very elements, whose quarrel it is folly to provoke and whose peace it is wisdom to seek; the frozen stores that Job cannot open are, in the Lord's hand, weapons ready to His word.
24:
The survey returns to the dawn's swift spreading, asking "by what way is the light parted, which scattereth the east wind upon the earth?" The reformed John Gill lays out the several ways the light may be said to be parted or divided: as at the creation, when God divided the light from the darkness; or at the sun's rising and setting; or between the two hemispheres and under the poles, where six months of light give place to six of darkness; or in the unequal distribution of day and night through the different climates; or even how, on one and the same day, the sun should shine in one part of the earth and not another, as once there was darkness over all Egypt and light in Goshen. Some, Gill notes, understand the verse of lightning rather than daylight, but he sets that aside, since the lightning is mentioned later.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, however, reads it precisely of the lightning and the thunder-cloud. Who can describe the cause and operation of a thunder-cloud, or the nature of the lightning itself — whether a simple or a compound substance, what its velocity, why it takes its zigzag form, and by what curious and unknown parting it is divided? This, he holds, is the difficult "parting" the verse intends; and "scattereth the east wind" he refers to kadim, the eastern storm, the euroclydon or levanter. Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, keeps to the daylight: the light is parted in being distributed in turn to all the inhabitants of the earth, and the east wind is naturally suggested by the origin of light, since dawn and the east wind rise together. John Wesley reads the same — the light variously distributed in the air and over the face of the earth, shining in one place and time and not another, all the effects of a wisdom beyond Job's reach; and the light, he adds, raises the east wind, for the sun the poets called the father of the winds, drawing up the exhalations that feed them.

So the witnesses genuinely divide over the "light" of the verse: Gill, Ellicott, and Wesley take it for the daylight, distributed and parted over the earth, while Clarke takes it for the lightning and its unaccountable path. Yet the argument is one whichever way the word is read. Whether it is the daybreak that shoots into every quarter of the sky or the bolt that forks unpredictably through the cloud, the parting of the light follows a way Job cannot trace, and the man who cannot say by what road the morning or the lightning travels is not fit to prescribe the ways of Providence.
25:
Here the divine speech turns a corner, and the witnesses mark it. Having proved Job's ignorance, the Lord now, as the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry observes, sets out in the same manner to show his impotence and weakness: as it is but little that Job knows, so that he ought not to arraign the divine counsels, so it is but little that he can do, and therefore he ought not to oppose the proceedings of Providence. The verse that opens this new demonstration asks who "hath divided a watercourse for the overflowing of waters, or a way for the lightning of thunder." Henry hears in it God's sovereign dominion over the waters: he has divided a water-course and directs the rain where to fall, even when the shower is most violent, with as much certainty as if it were conveyed by canals or conduit-pipes, so that every drop goes as it is directed; and he has the like dominion over the lightning and the thunder, which go not at random but in the way he appoints, since, as Psalms 135:7 says, he prepares the lightnings for the rain.

The reformed John Gill reads the "watercourse" not as any earthly channel or aqueduct such as men cut from the Nile, but as a course in the air or atmosphere, a canal for the rain to come down by; and this, he says, is the work of God alone, who so steers the course of the rain that it falls regularly and gently, not in spouts and floods, but in drops larger or smaller, on what spot of the earth he pleases. If Jarchi be right that every single drop has its own course and canal through which it passes, the wonder is greater still.

The wesleyan-arminian voices attend to both halves. Adam Clarke takes the "watercourse" from a root meaning to ascend, and suspects a cloud or even a waterspout may be meant, since the torrents of water can hardly be said to ascend except by evaporation, that divine contrivance by which the earth is both watered and dried; and "a way for the lightning of thunder" he renders "a path for the bolt of thunder," God directing even the course of the lightning, launching the bolt and making the path in which it is to run — a work heathenism gave to its supreme god, though none but the Almighty is truly the Thunderer. John Wesley reads the showers as coming down orderly and gradually, as if conveyed in pipes and channels, which without God's care would fall confusedly and overwhelm the earth; and the lightning and thunder as let out through a passage opened for them from the cloud in which they were imprisoned. Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, renders the opening simply, "cleft a channel for the water-flood." The witnesses do not divide: the rain that seems most lawless, and the bolt that seems most wild, are alike led along a way God cleaves for them, and the man who cannot cut such a channel in the sky cannot direct the God who does.
26:
The rain God directs falls even where no man will ever see it, "on the earth, where no man is; on the wilderness, wherein there is no man." The reformed John Gill draws the wonder out of the waste: the rain falls on land uninhabited by men, so dry and barren that there is no one to cultivate it and no one to reap any benefit from it, and yet the Lord sends it there for the use of the animals that dwell in those parts, which shows the reach of his care and providence even to the wild beasts of the earth. He hears in it, too, an emblem of the rain of the gospel falling upon the Gentile world, once a wilderness.

The wesleyan-arminian voices dwell on the same disinterested bounty. Adam Clarke observes that the thunder-cloud is conducted not only over inhabited countries, that the air may be purified and the rain sent down to fertilize the earth, but over the very deserts where there is no human inhabitant, and this to cause the bud of the tender herb to spring forth; for there are beasts and fowls and insects that inhabit the desert and must be nourished by the ground's produce, every tribe of animals being made by the hand of God and even the lowest of them supported by his kind providence. John Wesley reads the verse to the same point — that the clouds, broken by lightning and thunder, might pour down rain upon those parts where there is no man to water them by art and industry, as men do in cultivated places.

The witnesses do not divide, and their agreement lifts a great truth out of a small clause. The rain on the empty wilderness is providence at its purest, for here God can look for no return of service or of thanks; he waters a land where no eye admires the greenness and no hand gathers the fruit, simply because he is mindful of his creatures and will not let even the beasts of the waste go unfed. It is a rebuke folded into a comfort. Job had felt himself forgotten, a man singled out for suffering; but the God who remembers the untrodden desert and sends his rain where no man is has surely not forgotten the man who cries to him, and the bounty that spends itself on the wilderness is pledge enough that it does not overlook a suffering saint.
27:
The rain on the desert has a purpose the eye of man would never guess, "to satisfy the desolate and waste ground, and to cause the bud of the tender herb to spring forth." The reformed John Gill lingers on the doubled description of the ground — desolate and waste — two words heaped up to mark how exceeding barren it is, ground so dry and thirsty that it is like one of those things that never say "it is enough"; and yet God can and does give it rain to its full satisfaction. He hears in it a figure of grace, the Lord satisfying souls that are like dry and thirsty ground with the goodness and fatness of his house.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns it to the disinterested tenderness of Providence. The thunder-cloud does not only explode over inhabited countries, that the air may be cleansed and the fields fertilized, but is conducted over the deserts where there is no human dweller, and this to cause the bud of the tender herb to spring forth; for there are beasts and fowls and insects that inhabit the wilderness and must be nourished by the productions of the ground, every tribe of them made by God's hand, and even the lowest supported by his kind providence. John Wesley marks the movement of the argument at this point, observing that hitherto God had put such questions to Job as were proper to convince him of his ignorance, and that now he comes rather to convince him of his impotence: as it is but little Job can know, so that he ought not to arraign the divine counsels, so it is but little he can do, and therefore he ought not to oppose the divine providence.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill's parched ground that is never satisfied and yet is satisfied, Clarke's desert budding for the sake of its beasts, and Wesley's note that the questions are now bending from knowledge to power, all serve the one lesson of the verse. The God who quenches the thirst of a wilderness that can make no return, and dresses in green a waste that no man tends, is a God of a bounty and a reach past Job's comprehension and utterly past his imitation; and the very tenderness that spends itself on the desolate ground is the pledge that the God of the whirlwind, terrible as he is, is not an enemy but a giver of life even to the least of what he has made.
28:
The Lord presses the mystery of the rain to its source, asking "hath the rain a father? or who hath begotten the drops of dew?" The reformed John Gill answers that the rain has no father but God, and only God: however many the secondary causes, he alone is the efficient cause, the parent and producer of it; and the heathen themselves, he notes, gave God titles that owned as much. He that is our Father in heaven is the Father of the rain, and Gill hears in it a figure of the gospel, which likewise is not of men but of God, a gift come down from heaven, tarrying not for man, and a blessing as the rain is.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the question over and stays honestly baffled by the dew. Who is the father of the rain? he asks, having already traced some part of the apparatus by which God produces it. But "the drops of dew" — the small round globules, the egley or sphericles — set him among the disputes of the philosophers. Dew, he says, is a thin, light, insensible mist that falls with a slow motion while the sun is below the horizon; and various experiments have been made to settle whether it rises from the earth or descends from the atmosphere, with the learned inclining now this way and now that, so that the question is not yet decided. We cannot tell, Clarke owns, any more than Job could, which has begotten the drops of dew, the atmosphere or the earth. John Wesley keeps the question at its plainest and most humbling: is there any man that can beget or produce rain at his pleasure?

The witnesses do not divide. Whether they press the theology that God alone is the Father of the rain, or the natural philosophy that cannot yet say whence the very dew is born, they arrive at the one confession the verse is framed to draw. The rain and the dew, so common that men scarcely wonder at them, have no created father and no human maker; they are begotten by God, and the man who cannot beget a single drop, nor so much as tell where the dew comes from, is silenced before the God who fathers both. And Gill's turn to grace gives the verse its sweeter edge: the same God who is Father of the rain rains righteousness upon his people and is himself as the dew unto Israel.
29:
The imagery of parentage carries into the frost, "out of whose womb came the ice? and the hoary frost of heaven, who hath gendered it?" The reformed John Gill notes that the parent of the rain and the dew is the parent of the ice also, and he only; the ice is called elsewhere "his ice," his child, his offspring. And where the last verse had spoken of a father, this speaks of a womb, so that the Lord is here represented, Gill observes, as a mother — as Orpheus of old called God metropator, mother-father at once, both begetting and bearing the elements. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch draw out exactly this balance of the figure: rain and dew have no created father, ice and hoar-frost no created mother, and the parallel questions ask, on the one side after the one who begets and on the other after the one who bears, so that the whole generation of the weather is traced to God under both images at once.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns to the nature of ice and frost, and confesses how little the ages have added to Job's ignorance. Ice, he says, is a solid, transparent, brittle body formed of water by cold; some philosophers even suppose that ice is the natural state of water and its fluidity a real fusion, like that of metals under fire, so that water is by nature solid and made fluid only by heat. Ice is lighter than water, as eight to nine, owing to the air-bubbles produced in freezing, which is why it floats; and those bubbles acquire so great an expansive power as to burst the strongest vessels. The hoar-frost, meanwhile, is the congelation of dew, an assemblage of little crystals of ice of various figures according to the disposition of the vapours when the cold meets and condenses them, its production owing to laws we have not yet learned; so that of this whole subject, after the lapse of two or three thousand years, we know about as much as Job did, and the question "who hath gendered the hoar-frost?" is nearly as inexplicable now as then.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill's God who is both father and mother of the frost, Keil's careful balance of the begetting and the bearing, and Clarke's frank admission that science still cannot answer the verse, all converge on the one point: the ice and the hoar-frost, born of no creature, come from a womb Job cannot name, and the man who has never gendered a crystal of frost is confounded before the God who mothers the winter.
30:
The frost's work is shown in the sealing of the waters, when they "are hid as with a stone, and the face of the deep is frozen." The reformed John Gill draws the picture: the surface of the waters, by the frost, becomes as hard as a stone, so that it will bear great burdens and admit of carriages to pass over where ships went before, and the waters beneath are hidden and quite out of sight. He hears in it an emblem of the hard heart of man, which can only be thawed by the power and grace of God — by the south wind of the Spirit blowing upon it and the Sun of righteousness rising with healing in his wings.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets the verse in its winter season, noting that the very constellations named a little later rise in the winter months. The Hebrew word, he says, is understood by the versions generally to mean a hardening or congealing, and in intense frosts the ice does indeed become as hard as a stone; and "the face of the deep" is frozen not only in the polar circles but even in the northern countries — Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Holland, and parts of Germany — where the very seas are locked up from all the purposes of navigation for several months together. Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, would render the line "the waters hide themselves and become like stone": water loses its familiar quality, he says, and is turned into stone.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill's waters hidden under a stony lid, Clarke's frozen seas that bear the traffic of a continent, and Ellicott's water that hides itself and turns to stone, all fasten on the same marvel: that at the touch of the frost the most yielding of substances puts on the hardness of rock, and the restless deep is stopped and sealed. It is a change wrought silently and swiftly by a hand Job cannot stay, and it rounds off the argument of the winter's elements. The God who can lock the sea under a stone whenever he pleases is not to be commanded by the man who cannot melt a single sheet of ice; and if Gill's emblem holds, the same God who freezes and thaws the waters at his will can as easily break up the frozen heart, and warm what only his Spirit can warm.
31:
The divine speech now lifts above the clouds to the constellations, asking, "canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion?" The reformed John Gill takes the Pleiades as the seven stars whose rising in the spring brings the pleasantness of that season, an influence that cannot be restrained or hindered from taking its course; and he hears in it a figure of the irresistible influences of efficacious grace, which make a spring-time in souls that were before in the winter of darkness and death. Some versions, he notes, read "the bands of the Pleiades," as if the sense were, canst thou gather and cluster such a constellation together, as I have done? — and either way, Job can neither bind their sweet influence nor break their band.

The wesleyan-arminian voices identify the two constellations and their seasons. Adam Clarke describes the Pleiades as a cluster in the sign Taurus, six stars visible to the naked eye and seven to a keen one, appearing in the spring; and Orion, seen from the end of October through the winter, an elegant figure for winter itself, so that the Pleiades are set against Orion as the renewal of spring against the destruction of winter. Yet Clarke confesses a real reluctance here: he cannot follow the confident renderings of the learned, for he does not see the groundwork of the constellation-names and dares not draw conclusions from premises he doubts, recalling Coverdale's older version, "Hast thou brought the seven stars together? or art thou able to break the circle of heaven?" John Wesley reads it plainly — to bind is to restrain or hinder; the Pleiades bring in the spring and Orion, rising in November, brings in the winter; God can change their seasons, making the spring cold and the winter warm, but we cannot.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott weighs the phrase "sweet influences" two ways: it may refer to the supposed effect of the stars upon the weather, or the word may mean rather a chain or band, with allusion to their clustered group, "glittering like a swarm of fire-flies tangled in a silver braid" — and the parallel "bands of Orion," he judges, rather favours the second. So the witnesses genuinely divide over the "sweet influences": are they the astral powers the cluster pours out, as Gill and Wesley take them, or the very cords that tie the seven stars together, as Ellicott inclines? The question is left open, but the argument is not: whether Job cannot govern the influence of the Pleiades or cannot loose the knot that binds them, the seasons keep their appointed course above his reach, and the stars obey a hand that is not his.
32:
The tour of the heavens continues, "canst thou bring forth Mazzaroth in his season? or canst thou guide Arcturus with his sons?" The reformed John Gill weighs what Mazzaroth may be. He is inclined to take it for the same as "the chambers of the south," the southern pole with its stars, called chambers because hidden from our sight on this side of the globe, and named Mazzaroth from a root meaning to separate, because so separated and remote from us. Or else, he allows, it may mean the twelve signs of the Zodiac, each of which is brought forth in its own season — not by men, but by the Lord.

The grammatical-historical witnesses attend to the words. Keil and Delitzsch render the pair as the bringing forth of the signs of the Zodiac at the right time and the guiding of the Bear with its children, joining the question to the "ordinances of heaven" that follow. Charles Ellicott agrees that Mazzaroth is commonly understood of the signs of the Zodiac, and takes "the children of Arcturus" for the three stars in the tail of the Great Bear. John Wesley, the wesleyan-arminian voice, reads Mazzaroth of the stars in the southern signs, which Job cannot make to arise, and Arcturus of those in the northern, with "his sons" the lesser stars set round about and attending upon them as children upon their parents.

Against this settled range Adam Clarke, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, sets a wholly different guess. Mazzaroth is generally understood of the signs of the Zodiac, he grants, but Parkhurst derives the word from a root meaning to corrupt, and supposes it to name not a constellation at all but the pestilential wind, the simoom, whose season is the summer heats. So the witnesses genuinely divide over Mazzaroth: whether it is the southern constellations and the chambers of the south, as Gill leans; or the twelve signs of the Zodiac, as Keil, Ellicott, and Wesley take it; or, on Clarke's report of Parkhurst, the burning wind of the desert. The word keeps its secret, and that secrecy is itself the argument. Job cannot so much as agree what Mazzaroth is, still less bring it forth in its season or lead out the Bear and her train across the sky; and the man who can neither name nor guide the stars is in no case to guide the counsels of the God who calls them all out by name.
33:
The heavens come down to earth in the next question, "knowest thou the ordinances of heaven? canst thou set the dominion thereof in the earth?" The reformed John Gill takes the "ordinances of heaven" for the laws settled by God's own decree and purpose, firm and stable, respecting the situation, motion, operation, influence, and use of the heavenly bodies; laws so far from being made by men that they are not even fully or perfectly known by them. Man neither framed these statutes of the sky nor comprehends them.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the question upon the astronomer. Art thou a thorough astronomer? he asks; art thou acquainted with all the laws of the planetary system, able to account for the difference of the planets' motions and the influence by which they are held in their orbits, and to tell what dominion they exercise upon the earth? Sir Isaac Newton, he grants, gave much light on these things; but to his system gravity is essential, and what gravity is Newton could neither explain nor comprehend, nor are his followers one whit wiser; no man has ever yet fully found out the ordinances of heaven and their dominion over the earth. Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, glosses the "ordinances" as the recurring seasons and their power of influencing the earth. John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, reads them as the laws firmly established concerning the order, motion, and rest of the stars, and their powerful influences upon this lower world, and asks whether Job gave these laws, or perfectly knows them, or can manage and over-rule their influence.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill's decreed and unfathomed statutes, Clarke's confession that not even Newton could say what gravity is, Ellicott's seasons and their power, and Wesley's laws of motion and influence all converge on the single humbling truth. The heavens are governed by ordinances Job did not make and cannot comprehend, and their dominion is exercised upon the very earth he stands on by a rule he cannot set or alter. If man cannot so much as give an account of the laws by which the stars sway the seasons, how shall he pretend to know the counsels of God, or presume to teach him how to govern the world? The unreachable order of the sky is made the standing rebuke of every attempt to arraign the order of Providence.
34:
The Lord now turns from what Job cannot know to what he cannot do, asking, "canst thou lift up thy voice to the clouds, that abundance of waters may cover thee?" The reformed John Gill hears the question as a challenge to Job's authority over the sky.
