Can he, in a magisterial way, call to the clouds and demand of them that they let down rain in large quantities to water his gardens and fields and farms? He cannot: he may cry and call as long as he will, and not a cloud will stir, nor a drop be let down. For rain, Gill insists, is to be had only in a suppliant way, through the prayer of faith, as Elijah had it, and not in a dictatorial or authoritative way; the clouds and the rain are at the Lord's disposal alone. Ask of him, as Zechariah 10:1 bids — "Ask ye of the LORD rain" — and he will give it; but they are not to be commanded.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the verse as a contest of voices. Canst thou lift up thy voice to the clouds, that is, produce lightning and thunder so that water may be formed and poured down upon the earth? Thunder itself, he notes, is called in the Hebrew koloth, "voices," being counted the voice of God; so that here Job's voice, kolecha, is set in deliberate opposition to the voice of Jehovah, the feeble cry of a man against the thunder of the Almighty. The one can summon nothing from the sky; the other speaks, and the waters answer.

The witnesses do not divide, and between the two of them they draw the whole moral of the verse. Job cannot lift a voice that the clouds will obey; his loudest calling cannot fetch a single shower, for the heavens will not hear the earth unless God first hear the heavens. The rain that he needs and cannot command is to be sought, not seized — begged of God upon the knees, not ordered of the clouds by a word — and the very impotence of his voice against the thundering voice of God is the measure of the distance between them. A man who cannot call down so much as a passing shower to cover his own dry field has small ground to quarrel with the God who waters the whole earth at his pleasure, and every drought that drives him to prayer is a fresh proof of how poor and dependent a creature he is.
35:
From the rain the challenge passes to the lightning, "canst thou send lightnings, that they may go, and say unto thee, Here we are?" The reformed John Gill pictures the flash as a servant reporting for duty — gone where it was sent, its errand done, and back again to wait its master's further orders. But no man, he says, can dispatch such messengers, for the lightnings are only at God's command. He recalls the awful instances where they were made God's own instruments, and Elijah's calling down of fire from heaven upon the captains and their fifties; yet even that, Gill warns, is not to be imitated, for when the disciples desired the like upon a provocation they were sharply reproved by Christ in Luke 9:54. Were the lightnings at the beck of men, he adds, what dreadful things would be done in the world, since if good men when provoked would use such a power, much more would the bad.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the verse to the same effect and press its edge: what Jehovah here denies to the natural power of man is nevertheless possible to the power man has by faith, as the history of Elijah shows — a reminder that the impotence exposed is the impotence of the creature standing on his own strength. Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian voice, sets the verse against the pagan imagination of the thunder-god: the great god of the heathen, Jupiter the Thunderer, is figured grasping the forked lightning in his hand; but who can thunder with a voice like the Almighty? He is the Thunderer, and the very Hebrew word for the lightnings, berakim, Clarke notes, carries both sense and sound. "Here we are?" — will the winged lightnings be Job's messengers, he asks, as they are God's?

The witnesses do not divide. Gill's obedient flashes, Keil's word about the power of faith, and Clarke's true Thunderer all fasten on the one image: the lightning is God's willing servant, going at his word and returning to report, "Here we are"; and no man can so command it. Job cannot send a single bolt upon an errand, cannot make the fire come and go at his bidding; and the ministers of God's wrath will never be the ministers of his. The lightning that answers only to its Maker is one more of the mighty servants that surround the Lord and stand ready at his voice, and its instant obedience to him is the exact measure of its indifference to the man who would take his place.
36:
Amid the clouds and lightnings comes a question that seems to turn inward, "who hath put wisdom in the inward parts? or who hath given understanding to the heart?" The reformed John Gill takes it of the wisdom put into the inner man, the heart, as the next clause explains — such wisdom as would be needed to guide the stars, know the ordinances of heaven, and manage the clouds and the lightning; and no such wisdom, he observes, is put into man. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it of the understanding given to the contemplative person, and marks how little even the deepest thought can do without the inspiration of the Almighty: man knows nothing of his own mind, nor of the mode of its operations, possessing a power to conceive and understand that he cannot himself comprehend. Yet Clarke also reports the other readings the words have borne. Mr. Good would keep the passage among the lightnings — "who putteth understanding into the vollies, and giveth to the shafts discernment?" — while the Septuagint turns it aside to "the knowledge of weaving," and the Vulgate renders "understanding to the cock," that it might distinguish and proclaim the watches of the night.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott owns the difficulty frankly: the mention of the inward parts and the heart, set here in the midst of natural phenomena, perplexes every reader; and he offers as the natural solution to refer them, with Good, to the lightnings personified — "who hath put such understanding in their inward parts?" So the witnesses genuinely divide over what the "inward parts" are. Gill takes them for the mind of man, and the greater part of the versions with him; Good and Ellicott would make them the lightnings, given discernment to run their errands; while the ancient versions wander further still, to the weaver and to the crowing cock. Clarke, who has heard them all out, allows that either of the leading senses makes a good sense.

The witnesses do not divide over the point, however they read the parts. Whether the wisdom in question is the reason God has lodged in the breast of man, or the strange discernment by which the lightnings seem to know their way, the giver is God and none else; the soul that reasons and the bolt that runs its course alike have their understanding from above. And the humbling is the sharper if the human reading stand: the very faculty by which Job disputes with God was God's own gift, so that to turn it against its giver, and set up to be wiser than the Father of wisdom, is to abuse the one endowment that lifts him above the beasts.
37:
The survey of the sky nears its close with the clouds themselves, "who can number the clouds in wisdom? or who can stay the bottles of heaven?" The reformed John Gill takes the first clause of one who should have wisdom enough to count the clouds when the heavens are full of them, or to "declare" them — to set forth and describe their nature, their matter, motion, and use — which none can do completely; and he records the alternative that Aben Ezra and Broughton preferred, "who can make them as sapphire?", that is, who can make a clear and serene sky, of the colour of the sapphire, when it is overcast? — a thing none but the Lord can do.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke offers a like variation on the first verb, suggesting that the word rendered "number" may, as in the Arabic, mean rather to irradiate, and so refer to those celestial and inimitable tinges the sky sometimes wears; and the "bottles of heaven" he explains as the clouds, an allusion to the girbahs, the bottles of skin in which the people carry their water from the wells. Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, weighs the harder second clause, "who can stay the bottles of heaven?", and notes that it is understood in two opposite senses — either of pouring out the bottles or of laying them up in store — the context itself being uncertain, according as we read the sequel of thick mud or of hard, dry soil; and with this verse, he observes, the survey of physical phenomena comes to an end.

So the witnesses divide on more than one word. On the first clause, some take "number" at its face, some read "irradiate," and some, with Aben Ezra, "make as sapphire"; and on the second, Ellicott sets out the standing dispute whether "stay" means to empty the heavenly bottles in rain or to hold them back and keep the sky dry. The very uncertainty is a kind of argument. Job cannot even settle what the verse asks of him, still less number the numberless clouds or command the bottles of heaven to pour or to withhold; and the clouds that hang so near him, in his own atmosphere, keep their count and their contents as far beyond his reach as the stars beyond the clouds. The last of the questions about the sky leaves him, like all the rest, with nothing to say.
38:
The clouds' work on the ground closes the survey, "when the dust groweth into hardness, and the clods cleave fast together." The reformed John Gill reads the verse of the two states the earth may come to: the dust attenuated and ground, as it were, into powder, and the clods cleaving together as if glued, whether in a drought for want of rain, or when the bottles of heaven are unstopped and poured out upon it. It is the raining of the previous verses brought down to the soil, where the same waters that softened the ground may also, in their working, bake it into a solid mass.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the clause into a question about the deepest mystery of matter: who knows how the dust, the elementary particles of things, were first concreted, and how the clods, the several parts of the earth, continue to cohere? What is the principle of cohesion among the differing particles of matter, in all metals and minerals? Even water, in a solid form, enters as a part into several gems, their very water of crystallization. And he presses the wonder with a jeweller's care: how is it that ninety parts of alumine, seven of silex, and a little oxide of iron make the oriental ruby, or that silex and water form the precious opal, or that silex, alumine, carbonate and sulphate of lime, oxide of iron, and water combine into the lapis lazuli, or that a few worthless dusts grow into the emerald? These solids and fluids, of natures so different, the Almighty and infinitely wise God has grown into hardness and bound together in a way known and comprehensible only to himself.

The witnesses do not divide, few as they are here. Gill's baked clods and Clarke's cohering gems are two windows upon the one marvel — that dust should ever grow hard and hold together at all, whether in the clod of a dried field or in the crystal of a precious stone. The very ground Job walks on, and the jewels men prize, alike depend on a principle of cohesion he cannot explain; and the man who cannot say how a clod cleaves together, or how a ruby comes to be, is confronted once more with a wisdom that reaches into the least particle of matter as surely as into the courses of the stars. From the highest cloud to the hardening dust, the whole tour of nature has left the questioner without an answer, and with nothing to do but lay his hand upon his mouth.
39:
With the elements exhausted, the Lord turns to the living creatures, beginning with the fiercest, "wilt thou hunt the prey for the lion? or fill the appetite of the young lions?" The reformed John Gill marks the transition from meteors to animals, and the boldness of beginning with the lion, the strongest and most fierce and voracious of beasts. Who hunts his prey for him? Not man, who cannot, and who, if he could, would not dare; but the Lord does. Gill even reports the old notion that God has provided a small creature, a kind of jackal between fox and wolf, that goes before the lion and hunts the prey for him; and where the old lion is past going in search of food, the young lions hunt for him and bring it, or call him to partake.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it rather of the lioness or the strong lion, and turns the question upon Job's own faculties: hast thou the lion's instinct, dost thou know the habits and haunts of the creatures he seeks for his food? Job has neither the lion's strength, nor his instinct, nor his cunning, and could no more provide for him than match him. And Clarke notes a point of arrangement, that in the best Hebrew Bibles the thirty-ninth chapter begins with this verse, and rightly, since a new subject here opens, the natural history of the animal kingdom, where the foregoing chapter had treated of astronomy and meteorology. John Wesley reads the verse simply as another of God's wonderful works: is it by Job's care that the lions which live in desert places are furnished with their necessary provisions?

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agrees with Clarke on the division, that the new chapter ought to begin here, as the animal creation now passes under review. The witnesses do not divide over the sense. The lion that Job can neither feed nor face is fed daily by a providence that reaches even to the beasts of prey; and the God who hunts for the lion, and fills the mouths of its whelps, shows an all-sufficiency that spends itself as freely on the dangerous and the useless as on the serviceable. If Job cannot so much as cater for a single lion, he can hardly find fault with the government of a world in which the very lions are kept; and the care that stoops to the lion's den is a fresh witness that the God of the whirlwind is no niggard, but has a livelihood ready wherever he has given life.
40:
The picture of the lions is filled in with their lurking, "when they couch in their dens, and abide in the covert to lie in wait." The reformed John Gill considers whether these are the old lions, which for want of strength lie couchant in their dens or in some covert, waiting for whatever prey may pass; but he observes that the same haunts serve the younger lions too, and he cannot resist reading the crouching beasts as emblems of wicked men — cruel persecutors and bloodthirsty tyrants who fill their palaces and kingdoms with murder and rapine, lying in wait for their prey as the lion in his thicket.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the description forward toward the raven of the closing verse, and pause on the Hebrew wealth of names for the lion, of which they had spoken at ch. 4:10. They note that the word here can be used of the lioness, and that she is named first because it is hers to provide for the young ones, the whelps that couch with her in the den. Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian voice, draws out the natural history: the young lions couch and abide in the covert before they are able to hunt down the prey by open running, lying under cover to surprise the animals they are not yet swift enough to overtake; and from this very habit, he notes, the Hebrew word for the young lions, kephirim, takes its name, from a root meaning to cover or hide, as he had shown among the six names for the lion at ch. 4:11.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill's crouching tyrants, Keil's provident lioness, and Clarke's whelps hidden in the covert all keep to the one scene of the lion in ambush, and to the one argument that runs beneath it. The lions couch in their dens and lie in wait, and yet it is God, not their own craft, that fills their mouths; the whole apparatus of their hunting, the den, the covert, the patient waiting, is set within a providence that feeds them. Job, who could not provide for the lion, cannot even follow the beast to its lair; and the God who satisfies the desire of every living thing, down to the whelps crouching in the dark, governs a world whose least and fiercest wants are all within his care and none within Job's.
41:
The chapter closes on the least of creatures and the greatest of mercies, "who provideth for the raven his food? when his young ones cry unto God, they wander for lack of meat." The reformed John Gill answers in a word: not man, but God; he it is who feeds the ravens, creatures so voracious, mean, and useless, and yet not overlooked by their Maker. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke observes why the raven is singled out — chosen, perhaps, for its voracious appetite and its continual cry, which is the cry of hunger; a bird that dares not frequent the habitations of men, counted a bird of ill omen and hated by all. He finds the verse finely paraphrased by Dr. Young, whose lines have the young raven's brood, pained with hunger, calling importunately upon God, and asks who hears their cry and stills the clamours of the craving nest; and he notes the old fancy that the raven, by its clamorous and importunate voice, seems always to be calling upon Providence.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to the grammar of the last clause: "they wander for lack of meat" is not a direct statement but dependent on what goes before, so that the sense runs, "when his young ones cry unto God, when they wander for lack of meat." John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, marks the descent from the noblest of brute creatures, the lion, to one of the most contemptible, the raven, on purpose to show the care of God's providence over all his creatures, both great and small. The young ravens, he notes, are so soon forsaken by their dams that, if God did not provide for them in a more than ordinary manner, they would be starved to death; and he draws the comfort home — will he that provides for the young ravens fail to provide for his own children?

The witnesses do not divide, and the chapter ends where its whole argument has been tending. From the founding of the earth and the singing of the morning stars, through sea and death and snow and constellations, the divine speech comes to rest on a nestful of starving young ravens crying to God; and the God who has been shown so unsearchable in power is shown here so tender in care that he hears the cry of the meanest of birds and fills its mouth. If he stoops to the raven's nest, Wesley's question answers itself for Job and for every later reader: the God whose greatness has silenced all complaint is the same God whose goodness will not let his own people want, so that the very cry of the young ravens becomes an encouragement to trust him for our daily bread.
